title: Air Force security teams want to train with Chinese-made drones at nuclear base
gist: Task & Purpose reports that nuclear-security airmen at F.E. Warren Air Force Base are seeking to buy Chinese-made DJI drones under a Hegseth-issued exception, to train against the exact commercial drone technology adversaries are most likely to use, given DJI's dominant share of the global drone market.

themes.theme: DJI as the De Facto Threat-Representative Drone

insights.claim: The 90th Missile Security Operations Squadron at F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyoming, which is responsible for nuclear weapons security, is seeking Chinese-made DJI drones for training via a federal contract solicitation.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schogol
insights.so_what: A concrete case of a US nuclear-security unit deliberately procuring Chinese hardware despite broader US policy hostility to Chinese-made drones, an exception worth tracking within DoD's 'Blue' drone procurement policy.
insights.locator: Airmen with the 90th Missile Security Operations Squadron

insights.claim: The solicitation states nuclear-security airmen need DJI drones specifically to train with the 'exact devices adversaries are most likely to employ,' seeking six refurbished DJI quadcopters.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schogol
insights.quote: exact devices adversaries are most likely to employ.
insights.locator: nuclear security airmen at F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyoming, need

insights.claim: Samuel Bendett of CNA's Russia studies program calls DJI 'the new AK-47' for combat, saying no other drone brand can realistically simulate it because of DJI's battlefield ubiquity, simplicity and ease of use.
insights.speaker: Samuel Bendett (CNA), via Jeff Schogol
insights.so_what: Frames DJI as an entrenched, effectively irreplaceable battlefield training standard, implying continued demand for DJI hardware, and continued US policy tension, regardless of broader export or procurement restrictions.
insights.quote: DJI is like the new AK-47 for combat right now: simple, easy to use, great out of the box.

insights.claim: DJI, based in Shenzhen, China, builds most of the world's civilian drones and currently controls over 80 percent of the commercial drone market.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schogol
insights.so_what: Quantifies DJI's near-monopoly position, underscoring the difficulty of any Western de-risking from DJI hardware in commercial and dual-use drone markets.
insights.locator: DJI currently controls over 80% of the commercial drone market

themes.theme: The Hegseth Exception and Blue-List Drone Policy

insights.claim: Normally the U.S. military uses only 'Blue' list drones from government-vetted manufacturers, but the Air Force can purchase DJI systems under a directive issued last year by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schogol
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific policy mechanism, the Hegseth directive, that carved a training-use exception into an otherwise restrictive Blue-drone procurement regime, a precedent that could expand to other DoD units.
insights.locator: the Air Force can purchase the DJI systems under a directive

insights.claim: A Global Strike Command spokesperson said any DJI systems used for training would be 'completely isolated' from secure Defense Department networks, addressing the core security concern around Chinese-made drone hardware.
insights.speaker: Global Strike Command spokesperson, via Jeff Schogol
insights.locator: The spokesperson added that any systems used for the training

insights.claim: A justification document in the solicitation argues that without the specific DJI products, the squadron 'will be severely degraded' in its nuclear-security mission, because relying on Blue drones alone leaves operators untested against the actual radio-frequency signatures and proprietary protocols of 'the world's most prevalent drone threat.'
insights.speaker: Jeff Schogol
insights.so_what: Illustrates how deeply DJI's technical fingerprint (RF signatures, protocols) is embedded in real-world threat simulation requirements, reinforcing why substitute 'Blue' drones are seen as inadequate.
insights.quote: If these specific DJI products are not obtained, the [90th Missile Security Operations Squadron] will be severely degraded in its ability to execute its no-fail nuclear security mission.
insights.locator: Buying DJI brand drones is 'an absolute operational necessity'

insights.claim: Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, also home to U.S. nuclear weapons, is separately seeking DJI systems for counter-small-drone training, suggesting this is becoming a broader pattern across nuclear-missile bases rather than an isolated case.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schogol
insights.so_what: Signals a wider procurement trend across the nuclear triad's ICBM bases, worth tracking as a template that could extend further into DoD counter-drone training programs.
insights.locator: Officials at Malmstrom Air Force Base, Montana

themes.theme: Strategic Context: F.E. Warren's Nuclear Mission

insights.claim: F.E. Warren Air Force Base is home to the 90th Missile Wing, which maintains up to 150 Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missile launch facilities under Air Force Global Strike Command.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schogol
insights.so_what: Establishes the strategic stakes of the base being trained against Chinese drone technology; this is a core leg of the US nuclear deterrent, not a peripheral facility.
insights.locator: F.E. Warren is home to the 90th Missile Wing
